dataset.name: Soil biogeochemical properties and metrics of tree-mycorrhizal dominance for a 25-Ha forest in South Central Indiana, USA.
description: This data package contains a dataset used in the papers “Seeing the forest for all the trees: Mycorrhizal-associated nutrient economies are modulated by stem density and the synchrony between overstory and understory communities” and “Mycorrhizal associations of tree species influence soil nitrogen dynamics via effects on soil acid–base chemistry”. Four csv files are included along with a dataset. The dataset features chemical soil properties for a single sampling campaign within the 25 Ha Lilly-Dickey Woods Smithsonian Forest Global Earth Observatory (ForestGEO) plot in South Central Indiana, USA (ldw_dat_raw.csv). Also included are separate files focused on pH (pH_data.csv), carbon and nitrogen (CN_data.csv), and nitrification rates (Nitrification_data.csv). These variables are commonly associated with the tree-mycorrhizal dominance of forest stands. In these data subsets, each soil variable was matched to a 10 meter radius neighborhood wherein metrics of tree-mycorrhizal dominance (basal area, stem count, importance value, etc.) were calculated. Models between these soil variables and dominance metrics were used to investigate how different assessments of mycorrhizal associated nutrient economies (MANE) capture these relationships. This research was performed as a part of the Smithsonian ForestGEO project. This data package can be used to explore spatial variability in soil chemistry within a mature hardwood forest, or it can be combined with the included tree data, other fine-scale spatial information, or other tree inventory data for the site to evaluate how soil chemistry varies with tree community composition or edaphic or topographic properties.
On 2025-11-20, additional metadata were provided for this dataset: four data dictionaries and a file-level metadata file in comma separate (.csv) format.

measurementTechnique:
Soil sampling
Soil samples were taken at 253 locations evenly distributed throughout Lilly-Dickey Woods (LDW) and the coordinates of each sample was recorded in the summer of 2014 (Lin et al., 2022). At each sampling location a 0.25x0.25m2 subplot was established, the litter layer was removed, and three soil cores (5 cm diameter) were collected to 5cm depth and aggregated. Soils were sieved to 2mm in the field and two 4g samples of fresh soil were separated for net nitrification sampling before being transported to the lab for further processing.

Chemical analysis
Of the 253 locations sampled, soil pH was analyzed for 243 of these, potential nitrification rates for 240, and soil C:N for 126. Net nitrification rates were calculated as the change in 2M KCl-extractable nitrate (NO3-) during a 14-day aerobic jar incubation. An initial and final sample were prepared by placing 4g of fresh, sieved soil into each of two 15mL centrifuge tubes. The initial sample was extracted immediately with 10mL of 2 M KCl, shaken for 1 h, centrifuged at 3000 rpm and filtered through a Whatman no. 1 filter paper that was pre-leached with 2 M KCl. The final sample was incubated for 14 days in the dark at 23°C prior to extraction to allow microbial-mediated nitrification to occur. Incubated samples were covered with pierced Parafilm and dampened paper towels to maintain soil moisture while allowing for gas exchange. NO3- concentrations were measured colorimetrically using the cadmium reduction technique on a Lachat QuikChem 8000 Flow Injection Analyzer (Lachat Instruments, Loveland, CO, USA). For each sample, extractable NO3- was scaled to mg N g soil-1 using extract volume, sample mass, and moisture content. Net nitrification rates were calculated as final minus initial extractable NO3- divided by incubation length (14 days).
Soil pH and C:N ratio analysis was performed using air-dried soil. For soil pH, 5g of air-dried soil was placed in a 50mL centrifuge tube and 40mL of 0.01 M CaCl2 solution was added to the tubes. The suspensions were shaken for 30 minutes and vortexed immediately prior to analysis. Soil pH was measured using a benchtop pH meter and Thermo Scientific Sure-Flow Ag/AgCl pH electrode. Soil C:N was determined using 15-20mg of ground, air-dried soils measured into 5x8mm tin capsules and analyzed with a Costech-Elemental Analyzer to find %C and %N of each sample. C:N was then calculated by dividing %C by %N for each sample.
Soil available phosphorus was determined using the Bray extraction method, which uses an ammonium fluoride (NH₄F) solution to release labile P from soil. Extracted P was then quantified colorimetrically using a spectrometer. Soil exchangeable cations (Na, Mn, Al, Ca, Fe, K, and Mg) were extracted with barium chloride (BaCl₂). Concentrations were then quantified using inductively coupled plasma (ICP) spectrometry.

Comparison with tree data
We conducted all further statistical analyses in the R Statistical Software (v4.3.2; R Core Team, 2023). Using the coordinate data associated with the locations of the soil samples and the individual trees in the census, 10m radius neighborhoods (0.03ha) were constructed around each soil sample. We calculated the dominance of ectomycorrhizal (ECM) associated trees as a percentage of total basal area (BA), %ECM stem count (SC) dominance, %ECM importance value (IV), %ECM Overstory BA, %ECM Understory SC, canopy mismatch, and stand density for each circular neighborhood based on 2012 tree census data for LDW for all living trees (Johnson et al., 2018). We calculated %ECM BA dominance as the sum of the basal area of all ECM trees in the neighborhood divided by the cumulative basal area of all trees in the neighborhood. We calculated %ECM SC dominance by counting the number of individual ECM trees in the neighborhood divided by the total number of trees. We calculated an importance value metric for %ECM IV by averaging the %ECM BA and %ECM SC for each neighborhood. %E CM Overstory BA and %ECM Understory SC were calculated with the same method as overall %ECM BA and %ECM SC, however only considering trees >5cm diameter at breast height (DBH; overstory) and ≤5cm DBH (understory). The one tree species that has been reported to associate with both mycorrhizal types (Crataegus sp., 0.0001% of individuals in LDW) had half of its basal area and stem count dominance attributed to each mycorrhizal type at their location. We assigned mycorrhizal classifications (SI Table 1) according to designations from Phillips et al. (2013), Jo et al. (2019), and Soudzilovskaia et al. (2020). Canopy mismatch was calculated as the absolute value of the difference between %ECM Overstory BA and %ECM Understory SC. Stand density was calculated as the total number (i.e. count) of all stems ≥1cm DBH in the neighborhood.
Of the 253 soil samples, 112 had a second soil sample taken within 10m. To avoid overlapping tree neighborhoods, any two samples that were within 10m of one another were merged into one datapoint by averaging their coordinate data and soil variables. Tree neighborhoods were then calculated from the aggregated sample. Because of this subsetting approach, separate .csv files were generated for pH, C and N, and nitrification.
To isolate the effects of stand density and canopy mismatch, the residuals of the regression between stand density and canopy mismatch were used rather than the raw values of these variables. For simpler interpretation after residualization, the ranges of stand density and canopy mismatch were shifted by adding the absolute value of the minimum of each range so that the minimum value of each variable was zero (i.e. the range of stand density was shifted from –30.5-244 to 0-274.5).
To understand what groups at our site were driving the observed differences, we divided neighborhoods into four groups based on their overstory and understory dominance and compared the mean value for soil variables using a Sidak test. Neighborhoods were categorized into overstoryunderstory groups based on their overstory composition (AM [0-50% ECM overstory BA] or ECM [50-100% ECM overstory BA]) and understory composition (AM [0-50% ECM understory SC] or ECM [50-100% ECM understory SC]).
To test how canopy mismatch and stand density could inform relative metrics of mycorrhizal dominance, we calculated the relative contribution that stem count vs basal area based mycorrhizal dominance should have for each neighborhood. We predicted that as canopy mismatch and stand density increase, the increasing inclusion of %ECM SC data would result in greater predictive skill for soil variables relative to a model that calculates mycorrhizal dominance based on %ECM BA alone. To calculate this weight, we used min-max scaling to normalize the range of canopy mismatch and stand density to 0 - 1 scales. For canopy mismatch, which had a potential range of 0-100% in our datasets this was a straightforward approach (i.e. 10% canopy mismatch was a weight of 0.1 for %ECM SC). For stand density, which ranged from 0 to 274.6 stems after residualization (with a strong positive skew), we log-transformed the data, then rescaled to a 0-1 range. The rescaled values (“canopy mismatch weight” or “stand density weight”) were used to calculate weighted importance values where:
%ECM Canopy Mismatch Weighted IV = canopy mismatch weight × %ECM SC + (1 - canopy mismatch weight) × %ECM BA
%ECM Stand Density Weighted IV = stand density weight × %ECM SC + (1- stand density weight) × %ECM BA
In order to integrate the weights into a single mycorrhizal dominance metric, we created a single mixed canopy mismatch (CM) x stand density (SD) weighted metric (“ECMinformedIV”) by averaging %ECM CM IV and %ECM SD IV.
